problem: Most object navigation methods learn a single holistic representation covering exploration and navigation abilities, which is hard to interpret and hard to train. Skill-based approaches feed the same features to every skill, so the agent must still learn suitable features per skill.
motivation: Exploring unknown areas and approaching a discovered target need different information. Giving each skill its own dedicated representation could make training easier and the behavior more interpretable.
key_idea: SDRAM assigns each skill its own input representation: exploration uses high-level object representations plus a target embedding, and navigation uses detailed visual features, with a skill selection strategy choosing between them.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablation evidence can be cited. The abstract suggests that decoupling skills and tailoring features to each one, rather than sharing features, improves success rate and generalizes.
method: Skill selection strategy: chooses at each step whether the agent runs the exploration or the navigation skill.
Exploration skill module: takes high-level object representations and a target embedding as input.
Navigation skill module: takes detailed visual representations, as used in SOTA methods, to approach the discovered target.

setting.backbone: not specified in abstract (learned skill modules)

results: The abstract claims SDRAM outperforms SOTA models in AI2-THOR with a higher navigation success rate, and that the framework generalizes well. No numbers are given.
limitations: Only the abstract was available, so details and numbers could not be verified.
Evaluated in AI2-THOR according to the abstract; broader benchmarks are not mentioned.
